extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, and scientific method (philosophers, experimental scientists, advanced students)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative criteria and methods for correct reasoning, induction, and scientific investigation: how to form definitions, classify, construct propositions, infer causation, design experiments, and explain laws. The work is a systematic treatise on the logic of ratiocination and induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and province of logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the science and art of reasoning; more broadly, the science which treats of the operations of the human understanding in the pursuit of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes both analysis of the mental process (science) and rules for conducting it (art). Its province extends beyond syllogizing to naming, classification, definition, and other intellectual operations that conduce to knowing truths required in inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic concerns inferences, not intuitive truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is concerned with inferences (that is, conclusions drawn from premisses), not with truths known by immediate intuition or consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between what is known by consciousness (outside logic's domain) and what is concluded by reasoning (logic's domain). Beware mistaking rapid inferences (e.g., perception of distance) for intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with analysis of language: names and propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A preliminary analysis of language (names and propositions) is necessary before treating inference; names must be studied before things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revive and rationalize useful principles from older logic regarding classification of words, meaning, and propositional form because confusion about words impedes correct reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and kinds of names
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize types of names (general vs singular; concrete vs abstract; connotative vs non-connotative; positive vs negative; relative vs absolute; univocal vs equivocal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct classification of names is essential to avoid ambiguity and to ground accurate definitions and propositions; many errors in thought stem from neglecting these distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: nature and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition is a statement of the meaning of a name; definitions may be complete or incomplete and must be grounded on knowledge of the corresponding things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions of names should be based on analysis of meaning and, where practical, on acquaintance with the things named. Distinguish definitions from descriptions and ensure completeness where required for logical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and import of propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions have forms (affirmative/negative; simple/complex; universal/particular/singular) and assert relations (sequence, coexistence, simple existence, causation, resemblance) between ideas or meanings of names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the copula's nature and how different propositional forms convey different logical content; interpret propositions as assertions about relations between meanings or classes, not merely verbal transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real vs verbal propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish real (substantive) propositions from merely verbal ones; essential propositions are identical propositions, while accidental propositions are different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when a proposition states a genuine fact about the world (real) versus when it is merely analytic or verbal; two modes of representing a real proposition's import may aid this distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and role of classification (predicables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification involves genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens (the five predicables); kinds have a real existence in nature, and differentiae vary by purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classification sensibly for both general and technical ends; choose differentiae appropriate to the classificatory purpose to avoid misleading definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratiocination (syllogism) is a test/record, not the essence of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The syllogism (ratiocination) should be analyzed and understood, but it is not the fundamental form of reasoning; syllogism serves as a test and interpretation of the record of inferences from particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating the dictum de omni as the foundation of reasoning. Recognize that all genuine inference is from particulars to particulars; syllogistic rules interpret the record of such inferences rather than create new knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental axiom of ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a basic logical axiom underlying ratiocination (discussed as more fundamental than dictum de omni), which grounds valid inferential moves in syllogistic reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine and apply the true fundamental axiom rather than relying on outdated or erroneous theories that purport to justify syllogistic inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function and logical value of syllogism (criteria for valid deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllogism's function is to be a test of reasoning and a way to record inferential connections; its rules guide the interpretation of general propositions as summaries of particular-to-particular inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use syllogistic form to check the logical coherence of arguments; remember it is not the prototype of reasoning but a tool for assessing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trains of reasoning and the origin of deductive sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Trains of reasoning are series of inductive inferences (from particulars to particulars through marks of marks); deductive sciences arise when inductive generalizations become fixed and are then used hypothetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when a field can be treated deductively (because its laws are well-established by induction) versus when it must remain experimental and inductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration and necessary truths: conditional necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorems (e.g., geometry) are necessary relative to hypotheses; some axioms are experimental truths rather than purely a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat demonstrative (deductive) evidence as hypothetical: necessity follows from accepted premisses. Scrutinize axioms to see which are empirical and which are analytic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction: role and definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is the general method of ascertaining laws from observation and experiment; the logic of induction is essential for scientific inquiry and everyday reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate true induction from mere verbal transformation, spurious mathematical inductions, or descriptions. Recognize the task of generalizing modes of investigating truth and estimating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground of induction: uniformity of nature axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction rests on an axiom of the uniformity of the course of nature (subject to qualifications); simple enumeration is an insufficient form of induction in many cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge limitations of assuming uniformity in every sense; use more robust inductive methods than mere enumeration where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of laws of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: General regularity in nature is a tissue of partial regularities called laws; scientific induction must be grounded on prior spontaneous inductions and seeks simpler laws underlying complex phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek to resolve complex laws into simpler component laws; assess whether an observed regularity is a genuine law or a conjunction of conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of universal causation and criteria for causal inference
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of causation: every consequent has an invariable antecedent; the cause of a phenomenon is the assemblage of its conditions. Distinguish cause from invariable antecedent and consider permanent causes, simultaneity, and agent/patient distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infer causation by identifying unconditional invariable antecedents and analyzing the assemblage of conditions; beware simplistic identification of any invariable antecedent as the cause; consider compositional and temporal aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of causes (multiple causal modes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes often compose conjunctively; two principal modes are mechanical and chemical; composition is the general rule while simple proportional effects are exceptional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When investigating effects, consider combinations of causes and whether effects are proportional to causes; design inquiries to separate constituent causal actions where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation and experiment: steps and comparative advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: First step in inductive inquiry is mental analysis of complex phenomena into elements, then actual separation of elements (experiment). Experiments have advantages over observation and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with analytical decomposition, then choose observation or experiment depending on feasibility and the nature of the phenomena; use the advantages of each method appropriately (control in experiment; richness and breadth in observation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental method: identify a common circumstance present when an effect occurs (method of agreement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to detect potential causes by comparing multiple instances sharing an effect. Beware limitations when multiple causes or confounders are present; method of agreement is imperfect if causes intermix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental method: compare instances in which the effect occurs and does not occur, with circumstances otherwise the same (method of difference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides stronger grounds for causal inference when a single differing circumstance aligns with presence/absence of effect. Requires controlled variation; useful in experiment designs approximating 'all else equal.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine agreement and difference: identify a circumstance present in all positive cases and absent in negative cases to infer causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger than either method alone; used to triangulate causal factors by applying both presence-in-all and absence-in-none criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtract known causes/effects from a complex phenomenon to attribute remaining effects to remaining possible causes (method of residues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when effects are composite and component causes are partly known; relies on accurate identification of partial causal contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer causal relation when variation in one phenomenon is accompanied by variation in another (concomitant variations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful for quantitative causal relations but limited by potential confounders and nonlinearity; examine functional relationships and test for proportionality or consistent covariation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of the methods (plurality and intermixture of causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods have limitations: one effect may have several causes; causes can concur without compounding effects; some investigative cases make observation or pure experiment inapplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When causes compound or multiple agents act, simple agreement/difference may fail. Use combined, staged, or deductive approaches; recognize when purely experimental isolation is impossible and adapt methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-stage Deductive Method for complex effects
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Ascertain laws of separate causes by direct induction; 2) Ratiocinate from simple laws to complex cases (deduction); 3) Verify by specific experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction to obtain elementary laws, deduction to derive consequences for complex cases, and targeted experiments/observations to verify deductions. Verification is indispensable for robust scientific explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of laws: three modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation defined: (1) resolve a law of a complex effect into laws of concurrent causes and their coexistence; (2) detect an intermediate link in the sequence (mechanism); (3) subsume less general laws under a more general one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for explanations that reduce complex laws to simpler ones or reveal mechanisms; understand that explanations resolve laws into more general laws and that verifying intermediate links increases explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduction's role in science: verification and improvement of empirical generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Deduction, applied to well-established laws, yields new demonstrable consequences and explanations that can confirm, refine, or replace empirical generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deductive reasoning to generate testable predictions and to explain empirical rules of practice in terms of simpler laws (examples: agricultural practices, medical treatments). Always verify deductions by specific experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application: use of laws to find further instances and to explain phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a law is established, examine all cases presenting the necessary conditions to discover further instances and to explain related phenomena (e.g., Faraday's magnet-electricity, gas permeation across membranes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ established laws to predict new phenomena and provide deductive explanations; systematically search for contexts where conditions apply and test predictions empirically.
